Calibrate a self-signal against graded items

Source: R/core-signal-calibrate.R
hr_calibrate_signal.Rd

Measures how well a signal predicts that an item came out right, on a graded set, and fits a map from the signal to a probability. The result is a calibration record: it says how good the signal is, and it is the only thing hr_gate_threshold() and hr_apply_signal() accept as grounds for letting a signal gate an action. A new record is always advisory.

Usage

hr_calibrate_signal(
  signal,
  graded,
  key,
  method = c("platt", "isotonic", "none"),
  bins = 10L,
  split = 0.5,
  seed,
  B = 2000L
)

Arguments

signal

The signal's name, as recorded by hr_signal().

graded

The graded set, a data frame; see "The graded set".

key

A named list with the fields the record is valid for: served_model (the model the provider said answered, not the one asked for), version (the model version or snapshot), task, format, prompt_hash (of the prompt or template), effort, module (the reader or stage) and contract_version. Each is one string; NA is allowed except for served_model. A missing contract_version is filled with the running package's contract version.

method

"platt", "isotonic" or "none".

bins

Number of equal-mass bins for the ECE and the decomposition, held between 5 and 10.

split

Share of each cluster's items that goes to the fit half, strictly between 0 and 1.

seed

Seed for the split and the bootstrap. Required, so the same graded set always gives the same record. The caller's random state is left as it was.

B

Number of bootstrap resamples; 0 for no intervals.

Value

An hr_calibration: a list with signal, key, method, n_items, n_errors, n_unanswerable, n_clusters, accuracy (on the calibration half), metrics (a data frame of metric, estimate, lower, upper), selective_risk, decomposition, map (the fitted map), grid (the default thresholds for hr_gate_threshold(), from the fit half), data (the graded items with their half and mapped p), sample_design, bins (the number of ECE bins formed), B, seed, created_utc, created_by, status ("advisory" or "gating"), reasons, notes (remarks that do not stop a record from gating, such as a small cluster count behind the intervals) and gate (NULL until hr_gate_threshold() sets it). It has print() and as_json() methods.

The graded set

One row per item, with these columns:

score (or value)

The signal: a number, or a logical read as 1 and 0. Higher means more confident the item is right. The score column of hr_signals() is in this form.

correct

Whether the item came out right (logical, or 1 and 0). For an action such as "stop reading" or "accept", right means acting on the item was right.

answerable

Whether the item has an answer in its source. The set must include unanswerable items: a signal calibrated only on answerable questions has never been asked about the case where saying "I can answer" is most often wrong.

cluster

Optional: the document (or other unit) the item comes from. Without it each item is its own cluster.

item_id, signal

Optional. When signal is present only the rows for this signal are used.

split

Optional, as hr_assign_splits() and gr_read_labels() give it. When present only the rows in the calibration split are used: dev items were tuned on, and test items must stay unseen until they are scored. The rows left out are counted in notes and in a message, and a set with no calibration row stops with hr_bad_calibration.

Columns are matched by their exact names, so a column such as cluster_size is never read as cluster.

How it is computed

Within each cluster, a share split of the items goes to the fit half and the rest to the calibration half (a cluster's odd item goes to either side at random). The map is fitted on the fit half. Every metric, and the threshold search in hr_gate_threshold(), uses the calibration half, so the map is never judged on the items it was fitted to.

  • Platt scaling (Platt 1999) fits p = plogis(a + b * score) by logistic regression on the targets (N+ + 1) / (N+ + 2) for a right item and 1 / (N- + 2) for a wrong one, which keeps the fit finite when the halves separate. It is the default and the only fitted map allowed below 1000 graded items.

  • Isotonic regression (pool adjacent violators, weighted by the number of items at each score) needs at least 1000 graded items. The count is of the whole graded set before the split, so the map itself is fitted on about split of them (500 at the minimum with the default split). Between fitted scores it interpolates linearly; beyond them it holds the end values.

  • "none" takes the score as the probability, so it must lie in [0, 1]. It is the comparison that shows what fitting a map gained.

On the calibration half, with p the mapped probability and y 1 for a right item. The Brier score, its decomposition and the ECE judge p; AUROC2 and AURC judge the signal's own score, so they describe the signal and not the map. A Platt slope is free to be negative, and a map fitted to a signal that points the wrong way would otherwise rank well and hide it.

  • Brier score mean((p - y)^2), with its decomposition over bins of p (Murphy 1973; the two within-bin terms of Stephenson et al. 2008): brier = reliability - resolution + uncertainty + within_var - 2 * within_cov. reliability is the weighted mean of (mean p - mean y)^2 per bin, resolution the weighted mean of (mean y in bin - mean y)^2, uncertainty is mean(y) * (1 - mean(y)), and within_var and within_cov are the weighted within-bin variance of p and covariance of p and y. When p takes no more distinct values than bins, each value is its own bin, both within-bin terms are 0, and this is Murphy's three-part decomposition exactly.

  • AUROC2, the type-2 area under the ROC curve: the probability that a right item scores above a wrong one, ties counting half (the Mann-Whitney statistic), on the raw score. It measures ranking alone, and is below 0.5 for a signal that is higher when the item is wrong.

  • AURC, the area under the risk-coverage curve (Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017): items are accepted from the most to the least confident, and the error rate among the first k is averaged over k = 1, ..., n, in the order of the raw score. Tied scores enter together, each position taking the expected error rate under a random order within the tie. selective_risk gives the same error rate at 50, 80 and 90 percent coverage. Lower is better.

  • ECE, the debiased L2 calibration error over equal-mass bins (Kumar, Liang and Ma 2019): sqrt(max(0, sum_k w_k * ((mean p - mean y)^2 - mean y * (1 - mean y) / (n_k - 1)))). The plug-in error is biased upward by the noise in each bin's mean, and the subtracted term removes that bias, so a perfectly calibrated signal scores near 0 rather than at the noise floor. bins is held between 5 and 10. A calibration half of fewer than 10 items is lowered to fewer bins so each bin has at least two items. The ECE and the decomposition use the same bins, and items with the same p always share one: when p takes no more distinct values than bins, each value is its own bin, and otherwise an item's bin follows the average rank of its p. So the ECE does not depend on the order of the rows, and a signal with two values (a logical one, or any map of it) is measured over 2 bins. The record's bins is the number of bins formed, and reasons says so when it is below 5.

Intervals are 95 percent percentile intervals from a bootstrap that resamples whole clusters of the calibration half, B times. With fewer than two clusters in that half, or when every resample gives the same value, there is nothing to resample and the bounds are NA. With fewer than 20 clusters percentile intervals cover poorly, and notes says how many clusters they rest on.

A record is advisory until hr_gate_threshold() finds a threshold that passes. It also stays advisory when the graded set has fewer than 100 wrong items, when the fitted map does not increase with the signal (a Platt slope of 0 or less, or a flat isotonic fit), or when the ECE used fewer than 5 bins, as it does for a signal with fewer than 5 distinct values, such as a logical one; reasons says why.

References

Geifman, Y. and El-Yaniv, R. (2017). Selective classification for deep neural networks. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30.

Kumar, A., Liang, P. and Ma, T. (2019). Verified uncertainty calibration. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32.

Murphy, A. H. (1973). A new vector partition of the probability score. Journal of Applied Meteorology 12(4), 595-600.

Platt, J. (1999). Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines and comparisons to regularized likelihood methods. In Advances in Large Margin Classifiers, 61-74.

Stephenson, D. B., Coelho, C. A. S. and Jolliffe, I. T. (2008). Two extra components in the Brier score decomposition. Weather and Forecasting 23(4), 752-757.

See also

hr_gate_threshold(), hr_calibration_valid(), hr_signals()

Other signals: hr_calibration_valid(), hr_gate_threshold(), hr_signal(), hr_signal_policy()

Examples

# A simulated graded set: 40 documents, 10 questions each, a quarter of
# them unanswerable, and a signal that is informative but overconfident.
set.seed(1)
n <- 400
answerable <- rep(c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE), length.out = n)
truth <- stats::runif(n, 0.2, 0.95) * answerable
graded <- data.frame(
  cluster = rep(sprintf("doc%02d", 1:40), each = 10),
  score = pmin(1, truth + 0.15),
  correct = stats::runif(n) < truth,
  answerable = answerable)
key <- list(served_model = "mock-model-2026-01-01", version = "2026-01-01",
            task = "qa", format = "pdf", prompt_hash = "a1b2c3", effort = "low",
            module = "iterative")
cal <- hr_calibrate_signal("gr.iterative.can_answer", graded, key, seed = 7, B = 200)
cal
#> <hr_calibration> gr.iterative.can_answer: advisory
#>   400 items (235 wrong, 100 unanswerable) in 40 clusters; map: platt
#>   key: served_model=mock-model-2026-01-01, version=2026-01-01, task=qa, format=pdf, prompt_hash=a1b2c3, effort=low, module=iterative, contract_version=0.1
#>   calibration half: 200 items, accuracy 0.410
#>   brier   0.1598  [0.1305, 0.1920]
#>   auroc2  0.8393  [0.7791, 0.8918]
#>   aurc    0.3514  [0.2717, 0.4426]
#>   ece     0.0552  [0.0000, 0.1964]
#>   advisory: no gate threshold has been set

# The same split with no map shows what Platt scaling bought.
raw <- hr_calibrate_signal("gr.iterative.can_answer", graded, key, method = "none",
                           seed = 7, B = 0)
raw$metrics[raw$metrics$metric %in% c("brier", "ece"), ]
#>   metric  estimate lower upper
#> 1  brier 0.1843548    NA    NA
#> 4    ece 0.1690354    NA    NA
